title: Which buildings in Japan need a fire prevention manager, and what training is required?
description: Japan's Fire Service Act Article 8: which buildings need a fire prevention manager, the 10 hour Class A course, the 5 hour Class B course and the refresher.
shortAnswer: Article 8 of Japan's Fire Service Act requires the person with authority over a designated building, such as a store, restaurant, hospital or office with 30 or 50 or more occupants, to appoint a qualified fire prevention manager. Qualification is usually by completing a Class A course of about 10 hours or, for small buildings, a Class B course of about 5 hours. Managers of large specified use buildings must also take a 2 hour refresher about every five years.
keyTakeaways: Article 1-2 of the Fire Service Act Enforcement Order sets the thresholds: 10 or more occupants for residential care facilities, 30 or more for specified uses such as theaters, restaurants, stores, hotels and hospitals, and 50 or more for other uses such as offices, factories, schools and apartments.
The Class A new course runs about 10 hours over six subjects; the Class B course about 5 hours and is valid only for smaller buildings under 300 or 500 square meters.
The Class A refresher runs about 2 hours and is required for managers of specified use buildings that hold 300 or more people.
The manager must hold a managerial or supervisory position and must draw up and file a fire plan that includes fire prevention education.
Specified use buildings must hold firefighting and evacuation drills at least twice a year, with advance notice to the fire department.
jurisdiction: Japan (national, enforced by municipal fire chiefs and fire station chiefs)
regulator: Fire and Disaster Management Agency (FDMA) of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, with municipal fire departments
appliesTo: Owners, landlords and tenants with authority over the management of designated buildings
Employees appointed as fire prevention managers (bōka kanrisha)
Facility, office and store managers in retail, hospitality, healthcare, education, manufacturing and office buildings
Staff given roles in the fire plan, such as fire wardens and evacuation guides
Tenants in multi tenant buildings that each appoint their own manager

sections.heading: Which law requires a fire prevention manager?

blocks.text: **Article 8(1)** of the Fire Service Act (Shōbō Hō, Act No. 186 of 1948) requires the person with authority over the management (kangen) of a designated building to appoint a fire prevention manager (bōka kanrisha) from among people with the prescribed qualifications. The manager must prepare a fire plan and, under it, carry out firefighting, reporting and evacuation drills, inspect fire equipment, supervise the use of fire, maintain evacuation routes and manage occupant numbers.

The detail sits in the [Fire Service Act Enforcement Order](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/336CO0000000037) (Cabinet Order No. 37 of 1961) and the [Enforcement Regulations](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/336M50000008006) (Ministry of Home Affairs Ordinance No. 6 of 1961). As at November 2026 the provisions cited below are the current e-Gov text. The FDMA publishes related circulars on its [fire prevention management page](https://www.fdma.go.jp/mission/prevention/suisin/post16.html).

sections.heading: Which buildings need a fire prevention manager?

blocks.text: Article 1-2(3) of the Enforcement Order sets the threshold by use and by the number of people who enter, work in or live in the building, called the occupant capacity (shūyō jin'in). Uses are classified in Annex Table 1 of the Order.

blocks.text: Article 8(2) requires the person with authority to notify the fire chief or fire station chief without delay when appointing or dismissing a manager. In a building with several tenants, each tenant with its own authority over part of the building generally appoints its own manager, and Article 8-2 adds a joint supervising manager for high rise and other large multi tenant buildings.

sections.heading: Who can be a fire prevention manager?

blocks.text: Article 3 of the Enforcement Order requires two things: a qualifying credential, and a managerial or supervisory position that allows the person to carry out fire prevention duties properly. The second condition means a company cannot simply nominate a junior employee who completed the course.

For most buildings, called Class A buildings, the credential is completion of the Class A fire prevention management course run by a prefectural governor, a municipal fire chief, or a corporation registered with the Minister of Internal Affairs and Communications. Certain graduates in disaster prevention with one year of experience, and fire officers with one year in a supervisory post, also qualify.

Smaller buildings, called Class B buildings, can use a manager who completed the shorter Class B course. A Class B building is one with a total floor area under 300 square meters for specified uses, or under 500 square meters for other uses, provided it is not a residential care facility.

sections.heading: What do the fire prevention management courses cover?

blocks.text: Article 2-3 of the Enforcement Regulations sets the content and length of each course. The Class A new course (kōshu bōka kanri shinki kōshū) lasts about 10 hours and covers six subjects.

items: The meaning and system of fire prevention management.
Supervision of the use and handling of fire.
Inspection and maintenance of fire equipment, and maintenance of evacuation and fire protection structures.
Firefighting, reporting, evacuation and other drills.
Education needed for fire prevention management.

blocks.text: The Class B course (otsushu bōka kanri kōshū) covers basic knowledge and skills in the same six subjects in about 5 hours. The Class A refresher (kōshu bōka kanri sai kōshū) lasts about 2 hours and covers changes to fire prevention law over roughly the past five years and the study of fire cases. Article 2-3(5) requires the course provider to issue a completion certificate.

Delivery formats vary by provider. The [Tokyo Fire Department course page](https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/sk/kousyu.html) offers its combined Class A fire and disaster prevention new course either as an online course plus one day of practical training or as two days in person, the Class B course as one day in person, and the refresher online or as a half day in person.

sections.heading: Who must take the refresher, and when?

blocks.text: The refresher is required only for Class A managers of buildings covered by Article 4-2-2(1)(i) of the Enforcement Order: specified use buildings with an occupant capacity of 300 or more, which are also the buildings subject to annual fire prevention inspection reports.

The detailed schedule is set by the FDMA Commissioner under Article 2-3(1) of the Regulations. The [Tokyo Fire Department explanation of refresher deadlines](https://www.tfd.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/sk/kousyu_FAQ07.html) summarizes it in two cases:

items: If the manager completed the Class A new course or a refresher more than four years before the date of appointment, the refresher must be taken within one year of appointment.

Otherwise, the refresher must be taken within five years from the first April 1 after the most recent Class A course or refresher, and then repeatedly on the same cycle while the person remains manager of such a building.

blocks.text: Article 4-2-4(2) of the Regulations requires the building's fire prevention maintenance ledger to include a copy of the refresher certificate. Missing certificates are therefore visible at the annual inspection and to the fire department.

sections.heading: What must the manager do once appointed, and where does staff education fit?

blocks.text: Article 3-2 of the Enforcement Order requires the manager to prepare a fire plan, file it with the fire chief or fire station chief, and carry out fire prevention duties under it. Article 3(1) of the Regulations lists what the plan must cover; for Class A buildings this includes the self defense firefighting organization, fire equipment inspections, evacuation facilities, "education needed for fire prevention management" and regular drills.

Article 3(10) of the Regulations requires managers of specified use buildings to hold firefighting and evacuation drills at least twice a year, and Article 3(11) requires advance notice to the fire department for each. For other buildings, drills must still be held in line with the fire plan.

The maintenance ledger described in Article 4-2-4(2) must record the status of fire prevention education and of drills, along with inspections and equipment maintenance. That makes staff training records part of the building's statutory fire file, not just an HR record.

sections.heading: What happens if a building does not appoint a manager?

blocks.text: Under Article 8(3) of the Act, the fire chief or fire station chief can order the person with authority to appoint a manager. Under Article 8(4), the chief can order measures if fire prevention duties are not carried out in line with the law or the fire plan.

Article 42(1)(i) of the Act makes violating an Article 8(3) order punishable by imprisonment (kōkinkei) of up to six months or a fine of up to 500,000 yen, and the two may be combined in serious cases.

sections.heading: How should an organization manage fire prevention training across sites?

items: List every building or tenancy, its Annex Table 1 use, floor area and occupant capacity, and decide whether a Class A or Class B manager is needed.
Appoint managers who hold a managerial or supervisory role and track their course certificates.
Flag specified use sites with 300 or more occupants and calculate each manager's refresher deadline.
Build staff education from the fire plan, covering evacuation routes, extinguisher use and reporting, and record it for the maintenance ledger.
Schedule drills twice a year where required and file the advance notices.
Plan for succession, since a manager who leaves must be replaced and the new appointment notified.

blocks.text: A [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) can hold the manager, refresher and drill assignments, and [setting refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) covers the five year refresher logic. Workplace safety education under the [Industrial Safety and Health Act](/regulations/japan-industrial-safety-and-health-act-training) runs in parallel and is enforced by a different regulator.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each building as an entity with its use category and occupant capacity, so the framework derives whether a Class A or Class B manager and a refresher are required. Course certificates, refresher deadlines and education records attach to those obligations as dated evidence that can be exported for the maintenance ledger.

faqs.q: Can a company outsource the fire prevention manager role?
faqs.a: Generally the manager must hold a managerial or supervisory position in the building. Article 3(2) of the Enforcement Order allows an alternative for apartment buildings and other buildings set by ordinance where no manager can perform the duties, for example because all managers work far away, if the fire chief agrees. In that case the manager must meet ordinance conditions on authority and knowledge.

faqs.q: Does a Class B course certificate qualify someone for any building?
faqs.a: No. A Class B certificate qualifies a person only for Class B buildings: specified use buildings under 300 square meters or other buildings under 500 square meters, excluding residential care facilities. Larger buildings need a manager who completed the Class A course or holds an equivalent qualification.

faqs.q: Does a fire prevention course certificate expire?
faqs.a: The new course certificate itself does not lapse for most managers. Only Class A managers of specified use buildings with 300 or more occupants must take the refresher on the five year cycle. A manager who moves to such a building must check whether a refresher is due within one year of appointment.

faqs.q: Is fire prevention management the same as disaster prevention management?
faqs.a: No. Disaster prevention management (bōsai kanri) under Article 36 of the Act adds earthquake and other disaster duties for large buildings and has its own course. Fire departments often run combined courses that issue both certificates, as the Tokyo Fire Department does.
